pos: n. (in Presbyterian order, the court of elders governing a local congregation)
etymology: Latin sessio, a sitting, from sedere, to sit. A session is a body of men seated to judge — the name is a posture.
biblical_def: The session is the court of ruling and teaching elders in a congregation. Its warrant is a plurality: Paul “sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church” (Act 20:17) — plural, in one city — and Titus was to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). Its authority is judicial: “tell it unto the church… Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Mat 18:17–18). Its pattern is Jerusalem, where “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6). And its limit is Peter's: “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines session as a sitting or being placed; the actual sitting of a court or body of magistrates; and, in Scotland, the kirk-session, the lowest ecclesiastical court, consisting of the minister and elders.
webster_full: SESSION, n. A sitting or being placed.
2. The actual sitting of a court, council, legislature and the like.
3. The time or term during which a court, council or legislature sits.
KIRK-SESSION, in Scotland, the lowest ecclesiastical judicatory, consisting of the minister and ruling elders of the parish.
scriptures: And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
corruption_summary: A congregation is governed by one man or by a vote of the whole, and the New Testament gives a plurality of elders who are answerable and not sovereign.
corruption_paragraphs: Two arrangements are commoner than the one Scripture describes. In the first, a single pastor governs, with a board that advises and cannot restrain him; in the second, everything is decided by a congregational vote, so that a majority may overrule the men charged to watch for souls. The New Testament's pattern is neither: elders, always plural in a city, who rule (1Ti 5:17) and are themselves under the Word and subject to charges heard before witnesses (1Ti 5:19). An eldership that cannot discipline its own most gifted member has the first problem; a congregation that treats doctrine as a matter for a show of hands has the second.

The word is a posture and the posture is judicial, which is what makes the office uncomfortable. A session that has never had a hard case before it is either in a remarkable congregation or is not doing its work; Matthew 18 assumes that some cases will proceed to the whole church, and the promise of binding and loosing is attached to that process rather than to the elders' comfort. Where discipline has lapsed the session becomes a committee for buildings and budgets, which is the form most of them now take.
roots_summary: Greek presbuteros (G4245), elder; episkopos (G1985), overseer; proistemi (G4291), to rule, preside; deo (G1210) and luo (G3089), to bind and loose.
roots_lines: Greek presbuteros (G4245) — elder; Acts 14:23, 20:17, Titus 1:5, 1 Timothy 5:17, James 5:14.
Greek proistemi (G4291) — to rule, preside; 1 Timothy 5:17, 3:4–5, Romans 12:8.
Greek deo / luo (G1210, G3089) — to bind and loose; Matthew 16:19, 18:18.
usage: “Called the elders of the church” — plural, in one city.
“Tell it unto the church” — the process the binding promise is attached to.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” — the limit on the court.

pos: n. (a body of elders; in Presbyterian order, the court above the session, comprising the elders of a region)
etymology: Greek presbuterion, a body of elders, from presbuteros, an older man. The Authorized Version uses the word once, of the hands laid on Timothy.
biblical_def: “Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14) — a collective act by a body of elders, and the one occurrence of the word. The wider warrant for a court above the congregation is the council at Jerusalem, where a dispute that arose at Antioch was referred elsewhere and settled by “the apostles and elders, with the whole church” (Act 15:22), whose decision was then delivered to the churches to keep (Act 16:4). Elders are ordained in every church (Act 14:23), and Peter writes as one of them (1Pe 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines presbytery as a body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of all the pastors of churches within a certain district, and one ruling elder from each parish; also the Presbyterian religion.
webster_full: PRESBYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church.
2. A judicatory consisting of all the pastors of churches within a certain district, and one ruling elder, a layman, from each parish, commissioned to represent the parish.
3. The Presbyterian religion.
scriptures: Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
Act 16:4
And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed:
corruption_summary: Connection is treated as tyranny or independence as purity, and Acts 15 shows a local dispute settled by a wider assembly whose decree the churches then kept.
corruption_paragraphs: The independent objection is that no assembly stands above a congregation, since Christ is its head. The Presbyterian reply is Acts 15: a question arose at Antioch, the church there did not settle it, and the matter went up to Jerusalem, whose decision came back down as decrees for to keep, delivered to churches that had not sent delegates. Whatever one makes of the apostolic element, the shape is a court above a congregation, and Antioch's willingness to be bound is the part independents must account for.

The Presbyterian corruption is the mirror image and is at least as common: a court so heavy that congregations become branch offices, and so slow that a heresy is tried for a decade while a denomination bleeds. Peter's warning is aimed at courts as much as at pastors — not as being lords over God's heritage — and the whole apparatus exists for the flock rather than the reverse. A presbytery that cannot discipline a minister has failed at the one thing it is best placed to do, and the twentieth century's denominational collapses were mostly failures of nerve in exactly that court.
roots_summary: Greek presbuterion (G4244), a body of elders; presbuteros (G4245), elder; epithesis ton cheiron (G1936), the laying on of hands; dogma (G1378), a decree.
roots_lines: Greek presbuterion (G4244) — presbytery, body of elders; 1 Timothy 4:14, and of the Sanhedrin, Luke 22:66, Acts 22:5.
Greek epithesis ton cheiron (G1936) — laying on of hands; 1 Timothy 4:14, 2 Timothy 1:6, Hebrews 6:2.
Greek dogma (G1378) — decree; Acts 16:4, and of ordinances abolished, Colossians 2:14.
usage: “The laying on of the hands of the presbytery” — the one occurrence, and it is collective.
“They delivered them the decrees for to keep” — a decision travelling downward.
“The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder” — Peter's own rank.

pos: n. (an assembly of ministers and elders convened to decide matters of doctrine or order)
etymology: Greek sunodos, a coming together, from sun, with, and hodos, a way — men who travel together to one place.
biblical_def: A synod is a deliberative assembly of the church. Its model is Acts 15, where “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) after “no small dissension and disputation” at Antioch (Act 15:2); where there was “much disputing” before Peter spoke (Act 15:7); where James summed up the sense of the assembly (Act 15:19); and whose finding was issued in the most striking formula in church history: “For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28). The great synods since — Nicaea, Dort, Westminster — have claimed that pattern and, at their best, that modesty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines synod as a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an ecclesiastical council; and, among Presbyterians, the court next above the presbytery.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
2. A meeting, convention or council in general.
3. In astronomy, a conjunction of two or more of the heavenly bodies.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Act 15:2

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.
Act 15:7

And when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up, and said unto them, Men and brethren, ye know how that a good while ago God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel, and believe.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God:
corruption_summary: A council's decision is made infallible or made worthless, and Acts 15 shows an assembly that disputed much and then bound the churches.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 15 is untidy in ways that matter. There is dissension, disputation, and much disputing before anything is decided; Peter speaks from experience, Paul and Barnabas report, James reasons from Amos, and only then is a finding reached. A church that expects its assemblies to be serene has not read the chapter. Equally, one that treats the argument as the point — endless committees, nothing settled — has stopped at verse 7 and never reached verse 28.

The formula in verse 28 is the model and the guard: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us. Rome takes the first half and grants councils an infallibility; the modern church takes the second half and treats every decision as a provisional human opinion. The Reformed hold both with the order the Confession gives: synods are to determine controversies and their decrees are to be received with reverence if consonant to the Word of God — real authority, genuinely binding, and answerable to a higher text. Councils may err, and have erred; and a church without them settles nothing.
roots_summary: Greek sunodos, a coming together; sunerchomai (G4905), to assemble; sunago (G4863), to gather together; homothumadon (G3661), with one accord.
roots_lines: Greek sunago (G4863) — to gather together; Acts 15:6, 15:30, Matthew 18:20.
Greek homothumadon (G3661) — with one accord; Acts 15:25, 1:14, 2:46, 4:24.
Greek edoxen (G1380) — it seemed good; Acts 15:22, 15:25, 15:28, Luke 1:3.
usage: “There had been much disputing” — the chapter is untidy before it is decisive.
“It seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” — both halves, in that order.
“They delivered them the decrees” — a finding that bound churches which had not attended.

pos: n. phrase (a modern list of nine features of a healthy church, associated with Mark Dever and 9Marks Ministries)
etymology: From the 1997 book Nine Marks of a Healthy Church. The list is expository preaching, biblical theology, the gospel, a biblical understanding of conversion, of evangelism, of church membership, of church discipline, of discipleship, and of church leadership.
biblical_def: The nine marks are a modern diagnostic list, not a confession, and the texts behind them are ordinary: preaching the word (2Ti 4:2); the whole counsel of God (Act 20:27); the gospel defined and delivered (1Co 15:3–4); a church that is a countable body with a roll and a door (Act 2:41, 2:47); discipline that can put a man out and take him back (Mat 18:17, 2Co 2:6–8); and a plurality of elders (Act 14:23; Tit 1:5). The classical Reformation list is shorter — the Word rightly preached, the ordinances rightly administered, and discipline exercised — and the nine are best read as an expansion of the third.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mark as a visible line, character or impression made on something; a token, an evidence, a proof; a badge or distinguishing character.
webster_full: MARK, n. A visible line, character or impression, made on something by drawing, printing, cutting, stamping or otherwise.
2. A character or device; a badge.
3. A token, an evidence, a proof.
4. Notice taken; as, to take mark of a thing.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
corruption_summary: A useful checklist is treated as the marks of a true church, and the Reformers meant something narrower and more decisive by that phrase.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformation's marks of the church answered a life-and-death question: whether a given assembly was a true church at all, and therefore whether a man might leave Rome without leaving the church. The answer was deliberately minimal — the Word truly preached, the ordinances rightly administered, discipline exercised — because a mark that many true churches lack cannot be a mark. The nine are a list of health, not of existence, and confusing the two turns a helpful diagnostic into an instrument for unchurching congregations that are poor, small, or badly taught rather than false.

Used properly the list has done real good, particularly on membership and discipline, which most of the evangelical world had abandoned and which the New Testament plainly assumes. Used as a brand it produces the reverse: a network of churches that resemble one another in polity and style, and a young pastor with a checklist he applies to a congregation that has survived without him for a century. The last of the nine is a biblical understanding of leadership, and the first thing such an understanding produces is patience.
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), church; kerusso (G2784), to preach; prostithemi (G4369), to add, of members; epitimia (G2009), punishment, censure.
roots_lines: Greek prostithemi (G4369) — to add; Acts 2:41, 2:47, 5:14 — the church as a countable body.
Greek epitimia (G2009) — punishment inflicted by the many; 2 Corinthians 2:6, with restoration in 2:7–8.
Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint, ordain; Acts 14:23, 2 Corinthians 8:19.
usage: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” — the first of the nine, and the oldest.
“The same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls” — a church that could be counted.
“Sufficient to such a man is this punishment… ye ought rather to forgive him” — discipline with a door back in.

pos: adj. (producing the effect intended; in theology, of the call that infallibly brings the sinner to Christ)
etymology: Latin efficere, to work out, accomplish. An effectual thing is not merely aimed but lands; the theological term names a call that arrives.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses the word of prayer — “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jas 5:16) — of an opened opportunity, “a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries” (1Co 16:9), and of the gospel's working in the church (Eph 3:7; Eph 4:16; Phm 1:6). In theology effectual calling names the inward call that always arrives: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified” (Rom 8:30), an unbroken chain; and “All that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (John 6:37). The outward call may be refused; this one is the demonstration of “Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God” (1Co 1:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines effectual as producing an effect, or the effect desired or intended; or having adequate power or force to produce the effect.
webster_full: EFFECTUAL, a. Producing an effect, or the effect desired or intended; or having adequate power or force to produce the effect.
EFFECTUAL CALLING, in theology, that operation of the Holy Spirit by which the sinner is renewed and brought to Christ.
scriptures: Jas 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
John 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God.
For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.
corruption_summary: Effectual calling is heard as coercion, and the doctrine is that a man is made willing rather than dragged.
corruption_paragraphs: The old name for the doctrine was irresistible grace, and the word has done more harm than the teaching, because it suggests a man hauled to Christ against his will. The Confession is careful in a way the slogan is not: the effectually called are drawn to Jesus Christ, yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by His grace. The change is in the wanting. Nobody is saved reluctantly; the point of the doctrine is that the will itself, which was dead, is made alive, so that the man now desires what he formerly refused and comes without being forced.

Romans 8:30 is a chain with no dropped links, and it is the strongest single argument for the doctrine: whom He predestinated He called, whom He called He justified, whom He justified He glorified — the same company all the way through, and the calling in the middle must therefore be the kind that does not fail, since the number that arrives at glory equals the number that set out. That is not a Calvinist gloss on the verse; it is its grammar.

James 5:16 keeps the word from becoming abstract, and it corrects a common misuse in the other direction. The effectual prayer is not effectual because it is loud or long; the adjective attaches to a prayer that is energised, and the verse's own qualification is the character of the man praying. Effectual, in Scripture, is never about the force applied. It is about who is behind it.
roots_summary: Greek energeo (G1754), to work, be operative; energeia (G1753), working; kaleo (G2564), to call; kletos (G2822), called.
roots_lines: Greek energeo (G1754) — to be effectual, work; James 5:16, Galatians 2:8, Philippians 2:13.
Greek energeia (G1753) — effectual working; Ephesians 3:7, 4:16, Colossians 1:29.
Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call; Romans 8:30, 1 Corinthians 1:9, 2 Timothy 1:9; kletos (G2822), 1 Corinthians 1:24.
usage: “Whom he called, them he also justified” — a chain with no dropped links.
“They come most freely, being made willing by his grace” — the Confession, against the slogan.
“A great door and effectual… and there are many adversaries” — both clauses at once.

pos: n. (in Roman doctrine, a state of purifying suffering after death for those who die in grace but with temporal punishment remaining)
etymology: Latin purgare, to cleanse. Defined at the Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1563); unknown to the church of the first centuries in the developed form.
biblical_def: Purgatory is the Roman doctrine of a cleansing punishment after death, shortened by masses, indulgences and the prayers of the living. Scripture places the accounting immediately after death with nothing between: “it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). The believer's transfer is direct: “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise” (Luk 23:43); “absent from the body… present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8); “to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better” (Php 1:23). And the cleansing is already complete: “the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin” (1Jn 1:7); “by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines purgatory as a supposed place or state after death, in which the souls of persons are purified, or in which they expiate such offenses committed in this life as do not merit eternal damnation.
webster_full: PURGATORY, a. Cleansing; expiatory; tending to cleanse.

PURGATORY, n. Among catholics, a supposed place or state after death, in which the souls of persons are purified, or in which they expiate such offenses committed in this life, as do not merit eternal damnation.
scriptures: Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
corruption_summary: A second cleansing is added after death, and Hebrews says one offering has perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine requires a debt still outstanding after death for a person who dies in God's grace — guilt forgiven, temporal punishment remaining. Hebrews 10:14 is the sentence it cannot pass: by one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. If the offering perfects, there is nothing left to purge; if something is left to purge, the offering did not perfect. The thief on the cross is the historical test case, since no man ever had less opportunity to satisfy temporal punishment and no man was given a clearer promise: to day shalt thou be with me in paradise.

The doctrine's practical history is the reason the Reformation began in the way it did. Indulgences were the currency of purgatory, and Tetzel's traffic in them produced Luther's ninety-five theses; the first of which says that the whole life of believers should be repentance, and the twenty-seventh of which attacks the preaching that a soul flies out the moment the coin rings in the chest. A doctrine that turns the fear of the bereaved into revenue will not be reformed gently, and it was not.

The verse most often advanced for it is 1 Corinthians 3:15 — he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire — and the passage will not carry it. The fire there tries a man's work, not the man; it burns at the day of judgment, not in an intermediate state; and its outcome for the builder is that he is saved, not that he is purged. Scripture's only purgatory is the one that happened at Calvary, and it was not the sinner who went through it.
roots_summary: Greek katharizo (G2511), to cleanse; teleioo (G5048), to perfect, complete; hapax (G530), once; paradeisos (G3857), paradise.
roots_lines: Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse; 1 John 1:7, 1:9, Hebrews 9:14, Titus 2:14.
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to perfect, complete; Hebrews 10:14, 7:19, 9:9, 10:1.
Greek paradeisos (G3857) — paradise; Luke 23:43, 2 Corinthians 12:4, Revelation 2:7.
usage: “After this the judgment” — nothing named between the death and the judgment.
“To day shalt thou be with me in paradise” — said to a man with no time to satisfy anything.
“By one offering he hath perfected for ever” — the sentence the doctrine cannot pass.

pos: n. / title (Christ as the first to rise to an unending life, and so the head of a new humanity; rendering Greek prototokos ek ton nekron)
etymology: Firstborn, Greek prototokos. In Scripture the firstborn is not merely the earliest but the heir — the one who holds the rank, which is why Israel is called God's firstborn and why the birthright could be transferred.
biblical_def: “And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Col 1:18); “Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth” (Rev 1:5). The title is not about being the first ever raised — Lazarus and the widow's son preceded Him — but the first raised to die no more: “Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more” (Rom 6:9). Hence “Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming” (1Co 15:23), and Paul before Agrippa: “that he should be the first that should rise from the dead” (Act 26:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines firstborn as first brought forth; first in the order of birth; eldest; and, in Scripture, most excellent, most distinguished or exalted.
webster_full: FIRSTBORN, a. First brought forth; first in the order of nativity; eldest; as the first-born son.
2. Most excellent; most distinguished or exalted.
scriptures: Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Rev 1:5
And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood,
Rom 6:9
Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.
But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming.
That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should shew light unto the people, and to the Gentiles.
corruption_summary: Firstborn is read as first created, and in Scripture the word means the heir who holds the rank.
corruption_paragraphs: The Arian and modern Watchtower argument runs from Colossians 1:15, the firstborn of every creature, to the conclusion that the Son is a creature — the first one made. The word will not bear it. Prototokos in Scripture denotes rank and inheritance rather than chronology: God calls Israel my son, my firstborn, though Israel was not the oldest nation; Ephraim is made the firstborn though Manasseh was born earlier; and Psalm 89:27 says of David, I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth — of a man who was the youngest of eight. The three verses after Colossians 1:15 settle it anyway, since the reason given is that by him were all things created.

The title's force is in the second word. Others had been raised before Him and every one of them died again; He is the firstborn from the dead because His resurrection is the first that was permanent, and therefore the first that founded anything. That is why Paul immediately calls Him the head of the body: a new humanity begins where a man rises to die no more, and the firstfruits of a harvest is not merely the earliest sheaf but the guarantee and the sample of the rest.

The pastoral consequence is the one the funeral needs. If He is the firstborn, believers are the family, and the order is stated: Christ the firstfruits, afterward they that are Christ's at His coming. The Christian dead are not a separate case to be hoped for on general grounds; they are later members of a birth that has already happened once, in public, with witnesses.
roots_summary: Greek prototokos (G4416), firstborn; aparche (G536), firstfruits; arche (G746), beginning, origin; proteuo (G4409), to have the preeminence.
roots_lines: Greek prototokos (G4416) — firstborn; Colossians 1:15, 1:18, Romans 8:29, Hebrews 1:6, 12:23, Revelation 1:5.
Greek aparche (G536) — firstfruits; 1 Corinthians 15:20, 15:23, Romans 8:23, James 1:18.
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — firstborn; Exodus 4:22 of Israel, Psalm 89:27 of David, Genesis 48:14 of Ephraim.
usage: “The firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence” — rank, not sequence.
“I will make him my firstborn” — said of the youngest of eight.
“Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's” — the order for the funeral.

pos: n. phrase (the figure of God's judgment as a cup given to be drunk)
etymology: The image is one of the oldest in Scripture: judgment handed to a man in a vessel, so that he must take it into himself. Christ takes the figure up in Gethsemane and asks for it to pass.
biblical_def: “For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them” (Psa 75:8). Jerusalem “hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury” (Isa 51:17). Jeremiah is handed it for the nations: “Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations… to drink it” (Jer 25:15). It is poured “without mixture” at the last (Rev 14:10). And in the garden: “O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Mat 26:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cup as a small vessel used to drink out of; and, in Scripture, sufferings and afflictions, or the portion of blessings or of judgment allotted to a person.
webster_full: CUP, n. A small vessel, used commonly to drink out of.
2. The contents of a cup; the liquor contained in a cup, or which it may contain.
3. In a Scriptural sense, sufferings and afflictions; that which is to be received or endured.
4. Also, blessings and favors.
scriptures: Psa 75:8

For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.
Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out.
For thus saith the LORD God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it.

The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb:
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
corruption_summary: Gethsemane is read as fear of the nails, and the Old Testament had already defined what a cup in God's hand contains.
corruption_paragraphs: The agony in the garden is often explained as a brave man's dread of crucifixion, which raises a difficulty nobody answers: martyrs since have gone to worse deaths singing, and it would be strange for the Lord to face His less well than His servants faced theirs. The figure He used tells what He was looking at. A cup in the hand of the LORD is a fixed image in the prophets and it never means physical pain; it means the undiluted fury of God poured out on the guilty, drunk to the dregs. What made Him sweat as it were great drops of blood was not the Roman procedure but the contents of that cup.

The doctrine of substitution is the whole of the difference between the two readings. If He drank the cup, then the wicked of Psalm 75 who must wring out the dregs are the very people He drank for, and the exchange is total — His people receive instead the cup of blessing which we bless (1Co 10:16), and the same night He handed them one. Two cups sit side by side at the end of that evening: the one He took and the one He gave.

Revelation 14:10 keeps the doctrine from sentimentality by describing what remains for those who do not receive the exchange: wine of the wrath of God, poured out without mixture, undiluted. In this age every judgment is mixed with mercy and men mistake the dilution for the drink. The garden is the measure of what the undiluted cup is, and the measure is a Man on His face in the dirt asking whether there is any other way.
roots_summary: Hebrew kos (H3563), a cup; chemah (H2534), fury, heat; shemarim (H8105), dregs, lees; Greek poterion (G4221), cup; akratos (G194), unmixed.
roots_lines: Hebrew kos (H3563) — cup; Psalm 75:8, 11:6, 16:5, Isaiah 51:17, 51:22, Jeremiah 25:15.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — fury, hot displeasure; Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15, Psalm 6:1.
Greek poterion (G4221) — cup; Matthew 26:39, 20:22, John 18:11, 1 Corinthians 10:16, Revelation 14:10.
usage: “In the hand of the LORD there is a cup… the dregs thereof” — what the figure always means.
“Let this cup pass from me” — not the nails, the contents.
“Poured out without mixture” — what is left for those without the exchange.
